questions.stem: What is an industrial fermenter used for?

options.text: Growing microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi in large amounts
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Storage is not culturing.
Bread baking happens in ovens, not fermenters.
Filtration is a different process entirely.

questions.stem: Which food product is cultured in fermenters alongside mycoprotein?

options.explanation: Canning preserves; it does not culture microbes.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Biscuits are baked, not fermented in vessels.
Cave ageing is not the fermenter example.

questions.stem: Which medicine-producing moulds are grown in fermenters?

options.explanation: Insulation is unrelated.
Grapes involve wine making, not antibiotics.

options.text: Moulds that produce antibiotics such as penicillin
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Flavour moulds are not the antibiotic example.

questions.stem: Why is careful control of fermenter conditions the key advantage?

options.text: It makes the vessel cheaper to build
options.explanation: Control adds cost; the gain is reliability at scale.

options.text: It lets any organism grow anywhere
options.explanation: Control selects for the wanted organism only.

options.text: It removes the need for staff
options.explanation: Monitoring still requires operators.

options.text: It produces large quantities of exactly the right microorganism every batch
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A biotech firm wants engineered bacteria making a drug protein. Which vessel suits the job?

options.text: An industrial fermenter with controlled conditions for the engineered strain
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Open ponds invite contamination.
Dough mixing is a food process, not culturing.
Churns store; they do not control growth conditions.

questions.stem: State what fermenters are and what they grow.
questions.modelAnswer: Fermenters are containers used to culture microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi in large amounts.

questions.stem: Name two food products and one medicine linked to fermenter output.
questions.modelAnswer: Yoghurt and mycoprotein come from fermenters, and penicillin is harvested from moulds grown in them.

questions.stem: Explain why controlled conditions matter so much in industrial fermentation.
questions.modelAnswer: Microorganisms multiply only within narrow tolerances, so controlling the vessel keeps the wanted strain dominant and the yield high batch after batch.

questions.stem: A factory must switch its fermenter from penicillin to a GM protein run. What must change and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The vessel is steam-cleaned for aseptic restart, the nutrient mix is matched to the engineered strain, and temperature, pH, oxygenation and agitation are retuned so the new organism outgrows any contaminant.

questions.stem: Why is the fermenter cleaned with steam before a run?

options.explanation: Paddles need no steam lubrication.

options.text: To kill unwanted microorganisms so only the desired culture grows
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: To warm the vessel for the microbes
options.explanation: Sterilisation is about purity, not preheating.
Cleaning removes residues rather than dissolving them for use.

questions.stem: What is the role of the water jacket around a fermenter?

options.explanation: Oxygenation uses air input, not the jacket.
Paddles stir; the jacket regulates heat.

options.text: Maintaining the optimum temperature for enzyme activity in the culture
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Filtration is not the jacket's job.

questions.stem: How is the pH inside a fermenter corrected when it drifts?

options.explanation: Adjustment, not disposal, is standard.
Steam cleans, it does not neutralise pH.
Oxygenation does not correct acidity.

options.text: Acids or alkalis are added after the probe shows the drift
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Why must oxygen be supplied to most fermenter cultures?

options.text: The microorganisms respire aerobically to release energy for growth
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Sterilisation comes from steam, not oxygen.
Product texture is not the reason.
Paddle cooling is irrelevant.

questions.stem: What problem would a stopped stirrer cause in a working fermenter?

options.text: The pH probe would gain accuracy
options.explanation: Probe accuracy does not depend on stirring.

options.text: Nutrients, oxygen, temperature and pH would become uneven through the vessel
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Diffusion alone cannot keep large vessels uniform.
Stirring has no sterilising role.

questions.stem: State the aseptic precaution taken in industrial fermenters.
questions.modelAnswer: The fermenter is cleaned with steam to kill unwanted microorganisms and prevent contamination.

questions.stem: Name the probes used to monitor temperature and pH in a fermenter.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature probes and pH probes monitor the culture, with the water jacket and acid or alkali dosing making corrections.

questions.stem: Explain why enzymes in the culture need the temperature held at an optimum.
questions.modelAnswer: Enzyme activity peaks near an optimum, so a colder vessel slows the reaction while an overheated one denatures the enzymes and stalls growth entirely.

questions.stem: A batch grows unevenly, dense near the paddles and sparse at the walls. Diagnose the failing control.
questions.modelAnswer: Agitation has failed, because stirring paddles exist to spread microorganisms, nutrients, oxygen, temperature and pH evenly across the whole vessel.
